This article is all kinds of crazy. Not to say a lot of banks don't practice some shady practices but fractional-reserve is far from the worst or even hidden. It's in fact the whole basis of banks.

The banks don't just create money to lend. They can only lend money that they already have, either from customer deposits or by borrowing money from someone else (usually the central bank). So if somebody deposits 1 billion dollars they can't just magically create another 9 billion dollars and lend that out. They can do one of two things (or some combination). Keep the 1 billion untouched and borrow 9 billion from the central bank (now, how the central bank generates this 9 billion is another story) then lend that out or keep 100 million of the deposit and lend out the other 900 million. And this is all covered by your agreement with the bank. This is why they pay interest on your account. You are receiving part of the proceeds generated by lending out your deposits. And this is just on your cash deposits, any investments you have can't be touched by the bank although they carry their own separate risks.

That said, these numbers don't really apply to normal folk. In Canada at least, your cash deposits are guaranteed by the government up to $100k per institution. So even if there is a run on the bank and it collapses you will get at least $100k of your cash back. If you have more than that you can split it among multiple banks. If you have more than that you probably shouldn't be keeping it as a cash deposit anyway.

If you don't want the banks to "fraudulently" lend your money to others you can always cash your money out then keep it in a vault somewhere. Of course you won't make any interest off of it this way (and will have to pay the upkeep costs). Alternatively you can just invest it in treasury bonds. In bonds the bank can't touch it and if the government goes bankrupt you're shit out of luck anyway.
